  You can visit Mitla on two current Ada Tours programmes in Mexico: a five-day trip based in Oaxaca or a 12-day journey from Mexico City towards Yucatán. Both combine the archaeological site with the weaving workshops of Teotitlán del Valle, the mineral cascades of Hierve el Agua, and an introduction to mezcal production. The main differences lie in the wider geography, number of nights, and activities before and after the excursion.

## Which Ada Tours itineraries visit Mitla?

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) as a scheduled stop. Both routes include the ancient Zapotec site in the Oaxaca Valley, but suit travellers with different plans.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_oaxaca_city_break_five_days,tour_source_viva_meksika}}

**[Oaxaca: a Short Five-Day Journey](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/)** is suited to those who want several days in one region. All four nights are spent in Oaxaca. The itinerary includes a city walk, [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/), craft-producing villages, and a separate day combining Mitla with other attractions in the valley.

**[Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán in 12 Days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/)** covers a much wider area. Travellers explore Mexico City before Oaxaca and, after visiting Mitla, continue to Mérida, Maya monuments, and the Caribbean coast. Here Mitla occupies one day in a series of cultural and nature excursions.

The choice starts with a simple question: **are you primarily interested in the Oaxaca region or in travelling through several parts of Mexico?** The table's conditions apply to each full tour; the presence of Mitla on both routes does not make their other services identical.

## On which day is Mitla scheduled?

On the **five-day Oaxaca tour**, Mitla is visited **on day four**. After breakfast, the group travels to the palace buildings of the ancient city, then visits weaving artisans in [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/). [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/) and a mezcal distillery follow. The day takes approximately **9–10 hours**, departing at around 9:00–9:30 a.m. Travellers return to Oaxaca in the evening.

On the **12-day Viva Mexico journey**, this section falls **on day eight**. The route also combines Mitla, Teotitlán del Valle, Hierve el Agua, and an introduction to mezcal. The overnight stay is in Oaxaca, and the following day includes a flight to Mérida.

Both tours use the same [standalone Mitla, Weaving, Hierve el Agua and Mezcal excursion](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/). Its canonical description defines the sequence of the main stops and the core excursion arrangements. Our [Oaxaca page](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) is also useful if you want to explore the wider region.

## What exactly can you see in Mitla?

Mitla is best known for its **geometric stone mosaics** decorating the walls of ancient palace buildings. Small, carefully cut stones form stepped lines and repeating patterns. These distinguish Mitla from [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/), often visited by travellers the day before: Monte Albán is particularly striking for its open plazas, platforms, temples, and overall ancient city plan.

Among Mitla's prominent structures is the **Group of Columns**, where monolithic stone pillars survive. The walls reveal reliefs of different depths and traces of ancient finishing. The archaeological zone lies within the modern settlement of San Pablo Villa de Mitla, so exploring antiquity takes place alongside contemporary town life.

It is especially rewarding to have time to approach the patterns and study them up close. A quick view of the buildings from a distance reveals far fewer details. However, an extended independent exploration of the whole complex, separate museum visits, and additional stops **are not listed as standalone included services** of the selected tours; refer to the actual excursion day.

Mitla archaeological site should not be confused with the UNESCO property covering the prehistoric caves of Yagul and Mitla. They are different subjects, and the designation of one should not automatically be applied to the other.

## Why combine Mitla, crafts and Hierve el Agua in one day?

This route introduces three different sides of Oaxaca.

First, travellers explore Mitla's ancient architecture. Then, in [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/), they visit a family weaving workshop where local artisans demonstrate textile-making techniques and natural dyes. The excursion continues to [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/), where mineral deposits form white cascades resembling frozen waterfalls. Elevated viewpoints look out over the surrounding valleys.

The final stop concerns local mezcal production: the programme includes an introduction to the production process and a tasting. This is a defined part of the excursion, not a promise of unlimited tastings or a visit to any distillery of your choice.

| Stop | What is planned |
|---|---|
| [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) | Palaces and stone mosaics |
| [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/) | Weaving and natural dyes |
| [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/) | Mineral cascades and views |
| Mezcal distillery | Production and tasting |

In practice, this is **a full sightseeing day that includes transfers**. Set your priority in advance: more time among Mitla's ancient walls or a closer look at the other stops. Adding independent museums or workshops may require changes to the schedule.

## What is included and how do transfers work?

The [canonical excursion through Mitla](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/) includes **shared transport, a certified bilingual English- and Spanish-speaking guide, admission to the archaeological sites and Hierve el Agua, and a mezcal tasting**. Meals during the excursion, tips, and personal expenses are listed separately.

On the **five-day Oaxaca programme**, transfers between the airport and hotel on the first and last days are private, while excursions on days 2–4 and the transport included in them are shared. This is a significant distinction: private airport pickup does not mean a private guide and vehicle for every excursion. The tour also includes four nights of accommodation and breakfasts; one lunch is listed among the overall inclusions, although the published itinerary does not identify which day it belongs to. It is worth clarifying that when choosing the tour.

**Viva Mexico** combines different types of transfers and guided services across its longer route. The conditions for the Mitla excursion should therefore not automatically be applied to Mexico City visits, Yucatán journeys, or the domestic flight. Check the full inclusions and exclusions on the [12-day programme](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/).

Russian-language guiding is not specified for this excursion: the confirmed languages are **English and Spanish**. Also bear in mind that the excursion involves walking around archaeological buildings, moving between stops, and spending time outdoors.

## How to choose the right itinerary

| Priority | Suitable format |
|---|---|
| Several days in one region | [Oaxaca, 5 days](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) |
| Mitla and Monte Albán | Both routes |
| Mexico City together with Yucatán | [Viva Mexico, 12 days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) |
| A standalone sightseeing day | [Mitla excursion](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/) |

Choose the shorter journey if **you want to spend every night at one hotel in Oaxaca** and explore the region's history, craft traditions, and landscapes in depth. The five-day route has a separate historic-centre walk, a Monte Albán day with craft villages, and a Mitla day.

The 12-day programme is better suited to a first extended journey through Mexico, bringing together the capital, ancient cities, Oaxacan culture, and Yucatán. Its overall duration is greater because of the many other stops; time devoted to Mitla itself remains part of one excursion day.

If your main goal is Mitla itself, begin with the [archaeological destination guide](/mexico/place/mitla/). To compare the full geographic selection, see [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/) or [Mexico culture and history journeys](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours visiting Mitla

### On which day is Mitla visited on the five-day tour?

**Day four.** Mitla is combined with Teotitlán del Valle, Hierve el Agua, and a mezcal tasting. Travellers return to Oaxaca in the evening.

### When is Mitla visited on Viva Mexico?

**Day eight** of the 12-day journey. The day covers Mitla, craft traditions, and Oaxaca's natural attractions, while day nine includes onward travel and a flight to Mérida.

### How long is the excursion that includes Mitla?

The standalone excursion is listed as **9–10 hours**, including other stops and transfers. This is the duration of the entire excursion, not just the visit to Mitla archaeological zone.

### Is Hierve el Agua included?

Yes. Both named tours use an excursion module that includes [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/). Its conditions also specify admission tickets for this attraction. The programme does not promise swimming in all weather or unrestricted choice of time at the site.

### Are the guide and transport private?

**The Mitla excursion specifies shared transport and a bilingual guide.** On the five-day tour, private transfers cover airport arrival and departure, while excursion days use a group format. Compare the inclusions of the two complete tours separately.

### Can I visit Mitla without travelling all over Mexico?

Yes. The [five-day Oaxaca journey](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) includes Mitla while staying all four nights in the same city. For a specific day outing, see the [standalone Mitla excursion](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/).

## Mixquic: Day of the Dead in Mexico City, candlelight and family traditions

**Mixquic (San Andrés Mixquic)** lies in the Tláhuac borough of southeastern Mexico City. The community is known for its **Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead**, when people remember loved ones who have died. In late October and early November, families decorate their homes, prepare altars with flowers and photographs, and visit relatives' graves.

For visitors, a journey to Mixquic offers an opportunity to understand how a famous Mexican holiday is lived within a particular community. Streets fill with visitors and market stalls, but **family remembrance** remains at the heart of the occasion. Learning about local ceremonies therefore requires special consideration for people who have come to remember relatives rather than attend a tourist performance.

Mexico City's official tourism portal describes Mixquic as one of the city's most traditional places for the celebrations. The main dates are **November 1 and 2**, although some rituals begin earlier.

## What the Day of the Dead means in Mixquic

Mexico's Day of the Dead is associated with the belief that loved ones' souls return and with keeping their memory alive. Families prepare **ofrendas**, or household altars. These hold photographs, candles, food, water, and items that recall those who have died. **Cempasúchil flowers**, bright orange marigolds, are an especially visible part of the decorations.

Candles and flower-lined paths have a symbolic role, marking a way for souls to follow. For the family, the objects on an altar are personal memories; treating them merely as festive photo props misses their meaning.

In Mixquic, the festival has an especially strong connection with the cemetery. Relatives clean and decorate graves and spend time nearby. Outside visitors should remain observers and follow the community's rules.

## When the main events take place: October 31, November 1 and 2

The celebration unfolds over several days. Official Mexico City material describes Mixquic's own ritual calendar.

| Date | Main focus |
|---|---|
| October 31 | Remembrance of deceased children |
| November 1 | Family gatherings and altars |
| November 2 | The evening Alumbrada |

**October 31** is associated with remembering children. **On November 1**, families welcome and commemorate the souls of adults, prepare their loved ones' favourite dishes, and decorate places of remembrance. **On the evening of November 2**, **La Alumbrada** takes place: countless candles illuminate the cemetery as families remember their relatives who have died.

These dates mean different things. **Visiting Mixquic on November 1 does not automatically mean attending the Alumbrada on November 2.** If you are travelling specifically for the evening ceremony, check the precise date and time against the itinerary rather than relying only on the name “Day of the Dead”.

Preparations may begin earlier, but the best-known public events fall in late October and early November.

## What visitors can experience in the community

During the festival, Mixquic's streets change. Floral arrangements, altars, decorations, and local food stalls appear. Visitors may see families and neighbours preparing to remember the dead, while cultural events take place in some public areas.

The historic San Andrés church complex is one of Mixquic's landmarks. The official city tourism portal describes its colonial-era history and local religious traditions. Remember that functioning churches and cemeteries have their own rules of access.

The community is especially striking in the evening when candles are lit. Photographing in the dark among large crowds is difficult, however, and bright flashes or intrusive portraits can disturb people remembering their relatives. Understanding the meaning of what you see matters far more.

For another side of Mexico City's cultural programme, a festive trip can be combined with [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/) and [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/). These are separate districts and activities, so allow enough time for each.

## How to behave in the cemetery and during ceremonies

Respect for local residents is the most important rule of the visit.

- **Ask permission before photographing** people, family altars, and personal belongings.
- Do not step on graves, sit on gravestones, or enter areas closed off by relatives.
- Speak softly during prayers and commemorations, and do not use flash without permission.
- Keep pathways clear and never rearrange flowers just to improve a photograph.

Mexico's Day of the Dead is often associated with masks, face paint, and costumed parades. Celebrations look different in different cities. **Mixquic is particularly significant for its family traditions**, not for a compulsory carnival.

Official guidance from 2026 also recommends arriving early, allowing for traffic, and maintaining quiet during the Alumbrada. If a guide accompanies you, their role is to explain the cultural context and help you respect local restrictions.

## How to reach Mixquic from Mexico City

Mixquic belongs to Tláhuac in the southeast of the metropolis. Reaching it therefore requires planning: it is not a short walk from [the central Zócalo square](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/).

Visitor numbers rise sharply during the festival. Road access, temporary restrictions, and public transport arrangements may change. A travel time based on normal navigation estimates cannot be guaranteed during the events. It is especially important to plan your return journey for an evening visit.

On an organised tour, confirm the meeting point, departure time, length of the visit, and whether the return transfer after dark is included. If travelling independently, consult current city authority information about road closures and transport options.

## Mixquic on Ada Tours' Day of the Dead in Mexico itinerary

The [nine-day Day of the Dead in Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/) combines Mexico City, Teotihuacan, Puebla, Cholula, Atlixco, Mixquic, and Xochimilco.

**Mixquic is included on day six, November 1.** The programme begins with a trip to Atlixco before returning towards Mexico City for an evening visit to the festively decorated community. On that day you can see local altars, flowers, and traditions of family remembrance.

There is an important distinction: **the evening Alumbrada traditionally takes place on November 2**, while the itinerary above visits Mixquic on **November 1**. Attendance at the culminating November 2 ceremony therefore cannot be promised without changing the actual programme.

For other cultural journeys, see the [Mexico tour catalogue](/mexico/tour/), but the Day of the Dead is a seasonal event for which it is essential to choose an itinerary by specific calendar dates.

## Do you have to come in early November?

Outside festival season, Mixquic remains a residential community with its own history. However, the famous festive altars, evening candles, and large family commemorations are associated with a particular time of year. If seeing the Day of the Dead is your main purpose, plan for late October and early November.

Large visitor numbers bring queues and crowds. A quieter walk is possible at other times, but it will be a fundamentally different experience. Choosing an off-season date for photographs without crowds makes sense only if you are interested in the place itself rather than the festival.

## Frequently asked questions about Mixquic

### Where is Mixquic?

San Andrés Mixquic is a community in the Tláhuac borough of southeastern Mexico City, the capital of Mexico.

### When does the Alumbrada take place?

The traditional ceremony illuminating the cemetery with candles is held **on the evening of November 2**. Other rituals and altar decorations take place earlier, including October 31 and November 1.

### Can visitors photograph the altars and cemetery?

Follow community rules and ask permission before photographing people and family memorial spaces. Do not step on graves or interrupt commemorations for a photograph.

### Will we see the Alumbrada on the Ada Tours journey?

The current description of the [Day of the Dead in Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/) schedules Mixquic for **November 1**. The traditional evening ceremony on November 2 must therefore not be assumed to be included.

### Can Mixquic be visited without an organised tour?

It is technically part of Mexico City, but festival visits require careful planning of transport, the return journey, and local visiting rules. Traffic arrangements can change during large events.

## Which Ada Tours journey visits Mixquic?

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with [Mixquic](/mexico/place/mixquic/) on the main itinerary. This is the [Day of the Dead in Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/), a journey of nine days and eight nights built around the festival period from October 27 to November 4. It combines the Day of the Dead itself with museums, archaeological sites, and historic towns in central [Mexico](/mexico/).

Mixquic is scheduled **for day six, November 1**. In the morning, the group travels to [Atlixco](/mexico/place/atlixco/), then returns towards the capital and visits Mixquic in the evening. It is a long sightseeing day with two distinct stops. In Mixquic, the focus is on decorated streets, memorial altars, and the cemetery, where families gather to remember their loved ones.

Other days on the same tour include [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/), [Cholula](/mexico/place/cholula/), [Huaquechula](/mexico/place/huaquechula/), and [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/). The programme is particularly interesting for those who want to understand the festival through the family traditions of different places while also seeing historic and contemporary Mexico.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_meksika_den_mertvykh}}

## November 1 on the tour versus La Alumbrada on November 2

Mixquic, or San Andrés Mixquic in the Tláhuac borough, is known for one of Mexico City's most distinctive local Día de Muertos celebrations. Families prepare altars, decorate graves with marigolds, and bring photographs and favourite dishes of deceased relatives. It is especially clear here that the Day of the Dead concerns memories of particular people and family gatherings.

According to Mexico City's official tourism calendar, **La Alumbrada takes place on the evening of November 2**, when numerous candles are lit at the cemetery. Ada Tours' current itinerary specifies **an evening visit on November 1**. This offers an opportunity to experience Mixquic's festive atmosphere and traditions, but should not be taken as a promise to attend La Alumbrada the following evening.

If the November 2 ceremony is your main reason for travelling, first discuss a change to the dates and order of visits. Moving the evening affects transport, other excursions, and accommodation. Ada Tours can discuss a tailored option, but a particular ceremony is included only when it is confirmed in the agreed itinerary.

## Why visit on an organised itinerary?

Travelling independently from central Mexico City during festival days takes more time than a typical urban outing. Mixquic lies in the south of the capital, where large visitor numbers can bring traffic jams, restricted access routes, and changes to transport services. You also need to plan the journey back after an evening visit.

The tour day is arranged as follows: [Atlixco](/mexico/place/atlixco/) in the morning, Mixquic in the evening, and a return to accommodation in Mexico City. The tour includes private transfers and guided excursions with an English-speaking guide; check the exact stops and duration in the [Day of the Dead in Mexico itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/).

When discussing the journey, explain what matters most: observing a living festival tradition, seeing the capital's historic sights, or spending more time in the cemetery on a particular evening. Your priorities influence the dates and how full the day can reasonably be.

## What is included in the nine-day programme?

The tour price includes eight nights in the specified or similar hotels, breakfasts from day two through day nine, private transfers, excursions with an English-speaking guide, and admission tickets for sites listed in the programme. International flights, lunches and dinners, tips, and personal expenses are separate costs. Full conditions, group arrangements, and prices appear on the [tour page](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/).

The evening visit to Mixquic is only one part of a packed journey. Earlier days include ancient monuments and festival traditions in [Huaquechula](/mexico/place/huaquechula/); afterwards the programme continues in Mexico City and on the canals of [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/). The full route may be more than is needed for someone travelling solely for one evening event. For a first introduction to Mexican culture, it provides broader context.

## When to travel and how to prepare

Here the festival dates matter more than simply choosing favourable weather. For the tour described, **October 31, November 1 and 2** are important. Mixquic also has its own local stages of the celebration, so check what event falls on the evening you are scheduled to visit. If choosing a different year, confirm the current departure dates, available places, and festival schedule.

Comfortable closed-toe shoes, a light extra layer for the evening chill, a charged phone, and some extra time for traffic will be useful. You will be walking among residents, families, and visitors; photography can be sensitive. The city tourism authority asks visitors to seek permission before photographing people and family rituals, remain quiet during ceremonies, and avoid stepping on graves.

Treat Mixquic during the festival as a living place of remembrance rather than a stage set. Behave calmly, avoid disturbing families, and follow the instructions of local organisers.

## What can you compare with a tour visiting Mixquic?

If the Day of the Dead is your main interest, choose a route with festival dates, a Mixquic visit, and opportunities to see family altars. If you are mainly interested in archaeology and history, begin with [culture and history journeys](/interests/culture-and-history/) and [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/). For events, explore [Festivals and Events](/interests/events-and-festivals/): on this type of trip the date often matters more than the overall number of sights.

Consider the pace as well. Transfers, festive streets, and an evening walk can be tiring. When discussing a customised itinerary, mention your preferences for walking time, transport, and returning to the hotel so the proposed journey matches your expectations.

## Frequently asked questions about tours visiting Mixquic

### On which day does the tour visit Mixquic?

On the published Day of the Dead in Mexico itinerary, it is the evening of November 1, day six. Atlixco is visited first, followed by the return to Mexico City and the trip to Mixquic.

### Will we see the La Alumbrada ceremony?

It is not confirmed in the current programme: Mixquic is scheduled for November 1, while official information places La Alumbrada on the evening of November 2. Attendance requires a separately agreed date and itinerary.

### Can Mixquic be visited outside the Day of the Dead?

The community exists all year, but the tour described is tied to a particular festival period. Family altars, large evening gatherings, and other events cannot be promised for arbitrary dates.

### Does the programme only visit Mixquic?

No. It is a nine-day journey visiting archaeological sites, historic towns, museums, and districts of Mexico City. The complete sequence is published on the [tour page](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/).

### What format is suitable for a first visit to Mexico?

If you want to experience both the festival and other sides of the country, the full cultural route is more convenient. If your goal is one particular family ritual or the evening of November 2, discuss a focused individual itinerary before confirming the journey.

## Monte Albán: an ancient Zapotec city above Oaxaca

Monte Albán stands on a hilltop near [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) in southern [Mexico](/mexico/). A large area preserves monumental platforms, staircases, stone structures, and a ball court. The ancient ceremonial centre overlooks the valley and surrounding mountains.

The historic centre of Oaxaca and the archaeological site of Monte Albán were inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage property in 1987. The complex is principally associated with Zapotec civilisation, although its centuries-long history also reflects interactions among different Mesoamerican cultures.

## The main plaza and site layout

The extensive central plaza is surrounded by stone platforms and structures from several building phases. Their layout reflects the ceremonial and public functions of the ancient city. Different areas reveal its urban planning, architecture, and unusual hilltop setting.

According to UNESCO, Monte Albán's development involved terraces, engineered structures, and a complex architectural design adapted to the mountain landscape. This was a long historical process, not the construction of a single temple over a short period.

A guide can make the walk more rewarding by explaining the phases of development, the purposes of buildings, and aspects of Zapotec society. Without context, distinct ancient structures can easily look like similar pyramids.

## What to see on the route

Key features include the central esplanade, monumental platforms, a ball court, and carved reliefs known as the “Danzantes”. Researchers continue to discuss their historical meaning, so simplified tourist interpretations are best checked with specialists.

The walking route is outdoors. The sun can be intense, there is little shade in the main plaza, and the steps call for sturdy footwear. Bring water and sun protection. Check which parts of the site are open before visiting, as access may be restricted to protect archaeological remains.

Allow several hours to explore Monte Albán, plus separate travel time from Oaxaca.

## Combining the visit with craft workshops

A visit to the complex can be paired with the region's craft traditions. On the [five-day Short Oaxaca Journey](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/), Monte Albán is combined with workshops in San Antonio Arrazola and San Bartolo Coyotepec. Other days include Mitla and [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/).

Another option is the longer [Viva Mexico itinerary](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), which links Oaxaca, Mexico City, and Yucatán. Choose between them according to the time devoted to the ancient city itself and other regional sites.

Travellers interested in archaeology may also compare Monte Albán with [Mexico City and Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/). These complexes differ in history, architecture, and cultural origins.

## Frequently asked questions about Monte Albán

### Is it located in central Oaxaca?

No. The archaeological site stands on a hill outside the central urban neighbourhoods. You will need transport.

### Was Monte Albán built by the Maya?

The site's main historical tradition is Zapotec. Different cultures influenced the region, but Monte Albán should not automatically be classified as a Maya city.

### Can Monte Albán be explored in an hour?

An hour allows you to see only a small part of the site. For a meaningful visit, walk, and guide's explanation, allow several hours.

## Tours visiting Monte Albán: which itinerary should you choose?

Ada Tours offers {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include a visit to [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) on the main itinerary. Both focus on Mexican culture and history, but their structure is different.

[Oaxaca: a Short Five-Day Journey](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) suits travellers who want to concentrate on one region. All four nights are spent in [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/). The programme includes a historic-centre walk, an outing to Monte Albán and artisan villages, and visits to [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/), [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/), and [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/).

[Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán in 12 Days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) covers several historic regions. ## Why Monte Albán deserves a dedicated excursion day

The archaeological site sits atop a hill overlooking the Oaxaca Valley. It is one of the most important monuments of Zapotec civilisation. According to UNESCO, the city was inhabited for around 1,500 years, and the Zapotec capital flourished between the fifth century BCE and the ninth century CE. The site's later history also involved the Mixtec and other peoples of the region.

The most striking first impression is the space itself: a broad ceremonial plaza, stone platforms, temple foundations, and views across the valley. Monte Albán preserves a ball court, funerary structures, and reliefs bearing ancient figures and signs. Standing here helps visitors understand why the city's builders chose this elevated position overlooking the surrounding landscape.

The historic centre of [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) and Monte Albán have together formed part of the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1987. The two components belong to different periods: one reveals pre-Columbian history, the other colonial-era urban architecture. Visiting both on one trip helps you understand the valley's development over the centuries.

Our [Monte Albán destination page](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) explores the monument in more detail. Here the goal is to choose a tour that fits the archaeological site into your itinerary in the way you prefer.

## Monte Albán on the five-day Oaxaca tour

On the [regional programme](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/), day one is for arrival in Oaxaca and day two for exploring its historic centre. Day three includes Monte Albán and artisan settlements associated with local artistic traditions.

After the ancient site, the route introduces the work of contemporary craftspeople. In [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/), you discover the making of painted wooden alebrije figures, while [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/) is known for its black pottery tradition. This combination places archaeological heritage alongside crafts still practised in the valley's communities today.

Day four is devoted to other sites: archaeological [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/), weaving workshops in [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/), the mineral cascades at [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/), and an introduction to mezcal making. Day five concludes the itinerary with an airport transfer.

The five-day programme includes four nights of accommodation with breakfast, private airport transfers on arrival and departure days, and, on excursion days, shared transport, a certified English- and Spanish-speaking guide, and admission to the named sites, including Monte Albán. Additional excursions and international flights cost extra. Specific meal and accommodation conditions are available on the [tour page](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/).

This is a sensible option if you have already travelled around Mexico and want to devote several days specifically to Oaxaca, or if you prefer evenings in one city without constantly changing hotels.

## Monte Albán on the extended Viva Mexico programme

On the [12-day itinerary](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/), Monte Albán is scheduled **for day seven**. Before then, travellers explore Mexico City and its historic neighbourhoods, visit [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and other central Mexican sites, then reach Oaxaca.

Day seven combines Monte Albán, [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/), and [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/). The next day takes travellers through [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/), [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/), and [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/), before the journey continues towards Yucatán.

The advantage of this sequence is the opportunity to compare different archaeological cultures. [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and Monte Albán belong to different historic centres of Mesoamerica; later, travellers encounter other monuments in Yucatán. The longer journey involves more transfers and changes of accommodation, but covers a much wider area.

The programme includes eleven nights of accommodation, breakfasts, scheduled shared transfers and excursions, bilingual guiding, and entry tickets to historic sites. Domestic and international flights are not included in the price; compare the detailed pricing structure and services on the [Viva Mexico page](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) rather than assuming that the conditions of the neighbouring five-day tour apply.

## How to prepare for a walk around the ancient site

Much of the visit to Monte Albán takes place outdoors. Visitors walk between structures along stone paths and open plazas, with steps and uneven surfaces in certain areas. Consider in advance how comfortable this will be for people with limited mobility or young children.

Bring comfortable shoes, a hat, water, and sun protection. Even when the morning in Oaxaca feels cool, the sun is stronger on the exposed archaeological site, where there is less shelter than in the city. Weather changes through the year, and light rain protection can be useful during the wet season. Allow time for photographs and a thorough explanation from your guide rather than trying to rush between the platforms.

Monte Albán is outside the city centre, so transfers matter too. Both current programmes include it on an organised excursion day. However, transport arrangements and group formats differ: check the conditions of the particular tour you select.

Archaeological sites are administered by Mexico's INAH. Opening hours, restrictions on access to individual structures, and independent admission prices may change. If planning a visit independently, check these details shortly before departure. Including the site on an itinerary does not mean climbing every platform is permitted.

## Combining history, crafts and nature

On an Oaxaca journey, Monte Albán often provides the starting point for understanding the region. After its vast archaeological plaza, it is especially interesting to discover the crafts of [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/) and [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/). The historical theme shifts from ancient buildings to objects artisans still produce today.

The next contrast is [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) with its geometric stonework and the natural formations of [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/). They occupy a separate excursion day on both itineraries. This spreads the experiences across the journey rather than trying to see everything around Oaxaca in a few hours.

If you mainly want museums and city walks, choose according to the actual number of days in Oaxaca. If you want to add other regions, compare the [Mexico tour catalogue](/mexico/tour/) and [culture and history journeys](/interests/culture-and-history/), but remember: a Monte Albán visit is confirmed only on itineraries that explicitly include it.

## Frequently asked questions about tours visiting Monte Albán

### Which Ada Tours itineraries include Monte Albán?

It is included in the [five-day Oaxaca programme](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) and the [12-day Viva Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/). Archived routes do not appear in the current selection.

### Do I have to move to another city for the excursion?

The site is near Oaxaca and is visited on an excursion day with a return to the city. All nights on the short tour are spent in Oaxaca; on the longer programme, Oaxaca is one stage of a more extensive journey.

### How much time should I allow at the archaeological site?

Allow several hours to walk around the large open site, including the guide's explanations, transitions between areas, and photographs. The chosen excursion programme determines the actual stop duration; it cannot be inferred from the length of the entire tour alone.

### Are entrance tickets included?

Both programmes described include admission tickets to historic sites as part of their respective excursions. Compare the “Included” and “Not included” sections for your chosen tour.

### Which route is better for a first introduction to Mexico?

If you want to see Mexico City, Oaxaca, and Yucatán on one trip, the 12-day Viva Mexico itinerary is suitable. If your interests focus on Oaxaca, its ancient cities, crafts, and natural attractions, the shorter five-day route makes more sense.
